items.quote: So the messengers returned and reported to the king. Then the people went out and plundered the camp of the Arameans.
items.contrast: The messengers’ return and report immediately precede the plundering; following the Arameans to the Jordan occurs earlier.
items.reason: The question tests the order of events, and the transition “Then” uniquely identifies the report as the immediately preceding event.

items.quote: because he intended to leave the next day, kept on talking until midnight.
items.contrast: Paul’s impending departure is the reason he speaks so long; the lamps are only a detail about the setting.
items.reason: The explicit causal clause directly and uniquely supports the key.

items.quote: brought their scrolls together and burned them publicly.
items.contrast: They burn the scrolls after gathering them; calculating their value is reported afterward.
items.reason: The sequence uniquely supports the key, but “assembling materials” is an avoidably generic way to refer to bringing the scrolls together.

items.quote: They are ready now, waiting for your consent to their request.
items.contrast: The commander’s consent is the condition the ambushers are explicitly awaiting, while Paul’s being brought before the Sanhedrin would create the opportunity for the ambush.
items.reason: “Act” is vague enough to mean beginning the plan or actually attacking Paul, making both consent and Paul’s transfer plausible prerequisites. Asking what the ambushers are “waiting for” would uniquely recover the intended answer.

items.quote: The man of God had replied, “You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat any of it!” And that is exactly what happened to him
items.contrast: The officer is the person addressed by the prophecy and therefore the referent of “him”; the man of God is the speaker of the prophecy.
items.reason: Resolving the pronoun through the quoted exchange uniquely identifies the officer as the person trampled.
